title: Space resilience: what happens when satellites fail?
label: 16 November 2026 · Space resilience
summary: The committee examined how disruption to satellite services could affect shipping, communications and other essential services, and whether the UK is prepared for failures that spread across sectors. Witnesses highlighted poorly understood dependence on satellite signals, space debris, gaps in government coordination and the value of working with allies. They also stressed that large satellite networks can improve resilience but aren't a complete answer, and that the UK could do more to support its space businesses.

chapters.title: How satellite disruption could affect everyday services
chapters.takeaway: A loss of satellite signals could spread beyond space services and disrupt essential systems on Earth.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are the main risks if satellite services are disrupted?

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: We should look at what satellite services do for people and businesses on Earth, not just at satellites themselves. That means considering satellites, ground stations and user equipment, and how they connect. We also need to know what non-satellite systems could back them up.

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: My biggest concern is a failure spreading across several sectors, especially if it lasts. Positioning, navigation and timing (PNT) signals are a particular concern: jamming blocks them, while spoofing sends false ones. These methods are already common in active conflicts.

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: Ships rely on GPS not only to navigate, but also for communications and other onboard systems. In October, the Maritime and Coastguard Agency advised ports and shippers to consider how they would operate without it. Simply switching to paper charts wouldn't maintain the same efficiency.

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: In June 2026, 970 ships a day were being jammed in the Strait of Hormuz, and similar activity has been reported around the Baltic. We need to practise operating when signals are jammed or misleading, so we can find out whether our backup plans work.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We've heard that satellite services underpin 18% of the UK economy. Is that typical of a developed country?

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: I don't have comparative figures to confirm that. I can ask colleagues and provide information to the committee.

turns.speaker: Katie Barnes
turns.text: I don't have comparative economic figures either. At a discussion after a 2023 report, the national PNT office said the US and other countries were looking at reducing reliance on satellite navigation in some government departments and critical systems. I don't know how the UK compares economically.

turns.speaker: Katie Barnes
turns.text: I see two sides to the problem. Satellite communications can be an emergency backup when ordinary phone and internet services fail. At the same time, satellite signals are built into a huge number of everyday services, especially timing systems.

turns.speaker: Katie Barnes
turns.text: We may not know where all those signals are used or have plans for when they fail. Some systems act automatically when a signal arrives, without checking whether it's trustworthy. That's especially worrying for safety-critical systems such as automated vehicles and rail controls.

turns.speaker: Dr Adam Bower
turns.text: More satellites can help: a network with many satellites is less dependent on any single one. But that doesn't remove the risk of debris in orbit, which I think is greater than people often realise.

turns.speaker: Dr Adam Bower
turns.text: Satellites in a large constellation may be spread out, but they're often concentrated in particular orbital paths and heights. Taken together, their panels and equipment present a much bigger target for debris than each small satellite does on its own.

turns.speaker: Dr Adam Bower
turns.text: There isn't an equivalent of air traffic control for space. Operators have to manage the risk themselves, even as the number of satellites and pieces of debris grows.

chapters.title: Who should coordinate resilience in government?
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses said government needs a clearer, more joined-up way to understand how satellite services support many sectors.

turns.speaker: Baroness Kidron
turns.text: Does the space strategy do enough to prepare civilian services for disruption?

turns.speaker: Katie Barnes
turns.text: The strategy is mainly about growing the sector and encouraging participation. It doesn't say much about resilience, and defence seems to be the main stakeholder considered from that perspective.

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: The direction of the space strategies is good, particularly the effort to bring government departments together. But resilience mustn't fall between departments as those plans are put into practice.

turns.speaker: Baroness Kidron
turns.text: Do organisations that run essential services understand how much they rely on satellites, even indirectly?

turns.speaker: Katie Barnes
turns.text: Probably not enough. Satellite services support many critical sectors, so their importance isn't captured by looking at each sector in isolation. I don't know whether the government's information systems map these satellite dependencies or show how services could keep running if one failed.

turns.speaker: Katie Barnes
turns.text: Responsibility is spread across different organisations, and I don't see a clear place where the whole picture comes together. Satellite resilience barely features in the government's resilience action plan.

turns.speaker: Baroness Kidron
turns.text: Where should that responsibility sit?

turns.speaker: Katie Barnes
turns.text: I think national resilience needs a higher, unified place in government. A House of Lords report published today proposed a Cabinet-level minister responsible for resilience, with a preparedness lead in every department to turn that direction into action.

turns.speaker: Katie Barnes
turns.text: The government often starts from a list of known risks. But satellite services support many essential functions, and that dependence may not show up on the list. We should also ask what would happen if a service disappeared, not only what would happen if a particular listed risk occurred.

turns.speaker: Baroness Kidron
turns.text: Is enough being done with local authorities and community groups to understand and practise for severe disruption?

turns.speaker: Katie Barnes
turns.text: I don't know what has been done on this specific issue. More generally, people often don't know which services use satellites or where to find advice. The Royal Institute of Navigation has useful guidance, but someone would probably have to know to search for PNT resilience before finding it.

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: The national PNT office is a useful example of departments working together. Each department still owns its own risks, but the office coordinates ways to reduce them, including actions that can benefit several departments. I'm not saying every technology needs its own office, but this model shows what coordination can look like.

turns.speaker: Lord Arbuthnot of Edrom
turns.text: How well does industry understand failures spreading between sectors, and does it recognise the value of practising for them?

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: I don't have evidence about how industry as a whole sees this. But resilience changes over time, so exercises are a powerful way to test how well organisations can respond and recover, and to improve their plans.

turns.speaker: Catherine Atkinson
turns.text: Are the current government arrangements adequate for dealing with disruption to satellite services?

turns.speaker: Katie Barnes
turns.text: Not from a resilience perspective. Departments take responsibility for individual risks and sectors, but satellite services are used across many of them. What's missing is a reliable way to plan together before a disruption, not just coordinate a response afterwards.

turns.speaker: Baroness Tyler of Enfield
turns.text: Should the government set up a Cabinet group specifically for space, as the strategic defence review suggested?

turns.speaker: Katie Barnes
turns.text: A space group could bring together competing interests and make trade-offs clearer. But if we create one for space, we should ask whether other services that many sectors depend on also need this kind of attention. Civilian needs for satellite services aren't represented as clearly as defence needs in the current strategy.

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: Some central coordination is important, and it should focus on the services space supports on Earth as well as space itself. A National Audit Office review in March found confusion between departments and no agreed resilience levels for space weather. That's an example of resilience slipping between responsibilities.

chapters.title: Debris, large satellite networks and international rules
chapters.takeaway: Large satellite networks can spread risk, but their growth also increases collision risks and raises the need for shared rules.

turns.speaker: Lord Arbuthnot of Edrom
turns.text: Could bonds help pay to clear space debris?

turns.speaker: Dr Adam Bower
turns.text: I'm not familiar with the specific bond proposal. Companies, including the UK-linked firm Astroscale, are developing ways to remove particularly dangerous large objects from orbit. Some debris could also be avoided if operators designed missions to bring rocket parts back rather than leave them in space.

turns.speaker: Dr Adam Bower
turns.text: Financial incentives might help, but government contracts are currently supporting companies to develop and test removal technology. It's also a dual-use capability: a spacecraft able to capture debris could potentially be used to interfere with another country's satellite.

turns.speaker: Catherine Atkinson
turns.text: Some say large numbers of satellites improve resilience, while you warn that they add collision risks. How do you reconcile those views?

turns.speaker: Dr Adam Bower
turns.text: It depends on what the service needs. A system such as Starlink, which had more than 12,000 satellites in orbit by my last count, has a reason to be very large if it aims to provide internet around the world. But many communications or monitoring tasks might work with far fewer.

turns.speaker: Dr Adam Bower
turns.text: The concern isn't a particular number by itself. It's rapid growth and the concentration of more and more satellites in large systems. Governments should ask how many are actually needed for each task; changing satellite orbits may also help limit growth.

turns.speaker: Dr Adam Bower
turns.text: Four countries have deliberately destroyed one of their own satellites since 2007. An adversary could do that without directly attacking another country, but the resulting debris could damage other operators' satellites. Or debris could be created as part of a direct attack.

turns.speaker: Catherine Atkinson
turns.text: The international space rules are old and fragmented. What does that mean for the UK's resilience?

turns.speaker: Dr Adam Bower
turns.text: The main treaties were written before today's large number of commercial operators existed. There are also few agreed rules for military activity in space, even though military action can create debris that damages civilian services.

turns.speaker: Dr Adam Bower
turns.text: There may still be common ground. Debris threatens commercial, civilian and military operators, including the US and China, so countries have a shared interest in limiting it. The UK has helped lead discussions about responsible behaviour, including a proposed ban on tests of weapons that create debris.

turns.speaker: Dr Adam Bower
turns.text: There isn't a formal ban yet. The US voluntarily stopped such tests in 2022, and the UK and others have said they would do the same. It's a limited area where countries might cooperate despite broader disagreements.

chapters.title: Allies and the UK space industry
chapters.takeaway: International partnerships offer extra capability but create dependencies, while witnesses saw room for more ambitious UK support for businesses.

turns.speaker: Lord Tunnicliffe
turns.text: How much does resilience depend on international cooperation, and what if that cooperation breaks down?

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: Working with allies gives us access to more capabilities. If equipment on the ground can use different satellite networks and providers, one service can replace another when it is disrupted. But we need to understand those dependencies and make sure there are secure alternatives.

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: A strong UK space industry and skilled workforce also help. UK companies can develop useful capabilities for allies, and partners can help us in return. Working together adds resilience, though we need to know what we rely on.

turns.speaker: Katie Barnes
turns.text: Partnerships can be a relatively low-cost way to increase capability when interests are aligned. But if those interests diverge, maintaining the relationship and our place in it may take more effort. Partnerships bring benefits, but also dependencies and risks.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How well does the government support UK satellite businesses, and what more could it do?

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: There are good support programmes, and the Catapult helps promising businesses develop and grow. But the different forms of support could work better together. The government unit supporting the AI sector is an example: it brings together funding, computing access, help with visas and other support.

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: For space, that could mean bringing together access to skilled people and investment, business advice, grants, test facilities and regulators. The government could also make long-term purchases, becoming a dependable early customer for UK companies.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Could the government do more to help start-ups and growing firms get the money they need?

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: There's always more that could be done, although the government already has useful ways to support the sector.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Germany is reportedly investing much more. Should the UK show greater ambition?

turns.speaker: Lee Willcox-Jones
turns.text: Yes, the UK could be more ambitious in some key areas. I don't have figures to compare the UK and Germany directly, but I can provide written evidence on the comparison.
